meta.title: Angry or Compassionate?
meta.subtitle: The text of Mark 1:41 — witnesses, transmission models, arguments
meta.lede: When the leper says “If you will, you can make me clean”, almost every manuscript says Jesus was moved with compassion (σπλαγχνισθείς). Codex Bezae and a handful of Latin manuscripts say he became angry (ὀργισθείς). Most commentators think anger is original; most critical editions print compassion. This page lays out the evidence and the arguments so the reasoning can be traced step by step.

verses.greek: Καὶ ἔρχεται πρὸς αὐτὸν λεπρὸς παρακαλῶν αὐτὸν [καὶ γονυπετῶν] καὶ λέγων αὐτῷ ὅτι ἐὰν θέλῃς δύνασαί με καθαρίσαι.
verses.english: A leper comes to him, begging him [and kneeling] and saying to him, “If you will, you can make me clean.”

verses.greek: καὶ {σπλαγχνισθεὶς | ὀργισθεὶς} ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ ἥψατο καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· θέλω, καθαρίσθητι·
verses.english: And {moved with compassion | becoming angry}, he stretched out his hand and touched him and says to him, “I will; be clean.”

verses.greek: καὶ εὐθὺς ἀπῆλθεν ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἡ λέπρα, καὶ ἐκαθαρίσθη.
verses.english: And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.

verses.greek: καὶ ἐμβριμησάμενος αὐτῷ εὐθὺς ἐξέβαλεν αὐτόν
verses.english: And sternly warning him (lit. “snorting at him”), he immediately drove him out
verses.note: ἐμβριμησάμενος and ἐξέβαλεν are the harsh words that figure in many of the arguments below.

verses.greek: καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· ὅρα μηδενὶ μηδὲν εἴπῃς, ἀλλ᾿ ὕπαγε σεαυτὸν δεῖξον τῷ ἱερεῖ καὶ προσένεγκε περὶ τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ σου ἃ προσέταξεν Μωϋσῆς, εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς.
verses.english: and says to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone; but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”

verses.greek: Ὁ δὲ ἐξελθὼν ἤρξατο κηρύσσειν πολλὰ καὶ διαφημίζειν τὸν λόγον, ὥστε μηκέτι αὐτὸν δύνασθαι φανερῶς εἰς πόλιν εἰσελθεῖν, ἀλλ᾿ ἔξω ἐπ᾿ ἐρήμοις τόποις ἦν· καὶ ἤρχοντο πρὸς αὐτὸν πάντοθεν.
verses.english: But he went out and began to proclaim it freely and to spread the word, so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly but stayed out in deserted places; and they came to him from everywhere.

καὶ ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα ἥψατο αὐτοῦ λέγων· θέλω, καθαρίσθητι

na28.apparatusTranscription: • 41 ⸀ ο δε Ιησους A C K (L) W Γ Δ Θ 0130 f1.13 28. 565. 579. 700. 1241. 1424. 2542. l2211 𝔐 lat sy sa-ms bo-pt ¦ txt ℵ B D 892 it sa-mss bo-pt | ⸁ οργισθεις D a ff² r¹*
howToRead: The first unit concerns only the opening words: most manuscripts read ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς (“But Jesus”), while ℵ B D 892 and most Old Latin manuscripts read καί (“And”), which NA28 prints.

The second unit is the one at issue. NA28 lists only the witnesses against its text: ὀργισθείς is read by D (Codex Bezae) and the Old Latin manuscripts a, ff² and r¹ (first hand, marked *). Every other witness is implied for σπλαγχνισθείς.
Notice that Bezae sides with ℵ and B in the first unit (καί) and stands alone among Greek manuscripts in the second.

witnesses.summary: No papyrus preserves this verse (P137 covers Mark 1:7–9 and 16–18 only; P45 begins in Mark 4). The earliest Greek evidence is from the fourth century.

count.text: In Text und Textwert, 1623 of 1631 Greek manuscripts read σπλαγχνισθείς at this test passage.

items.name: Codex Bezae Cantabrigiensis
items.attests: καὶ ὀργισθεὶς ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ ἥψατο αὐτοῦ
items.note: The only Greek manuscript with this reading.

items.name: Codex Bezae, Latin column
items.attests: et iratus extendit manum suam et tetigit eum
items.note: Facing Latin page of the same codex.

items.name: Codex Usserianus Primus
items.note: First hand only. A later hand added mis- above the line and deleted the a: iratus → misiratus → misirtus (= misertus).

groups.title: Both: compassion and anger
groups.reading: ܐܬܪܚܡ ܥܠܘܗܝ ܘܟܕ ܡܦܪ — “had compassion on him and, being angered, …”

items.name: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on the Gospel Harmony (Diatessaron) XII.21–24
items.attests: “Our Lord was angry, therefore, about both things” … “reproof through his anger, and compassion through his healing” … “again, it is said that he was not angry with him, but with his leprosy.”
items.note: Ephrem explains a text that had both emotions. The key word mpār (“being angered”) was mistranslated in the standard editions (Leloir: succendebat; McCarthy: “was refuting”), so its status as a gospel citation was missed until Taylor 2020.

items.name: Old Syriac Gospels, fragmentary palimpsest (Sinai Syr. NF 37 + NF 39)
items.attests: “Now he, Jesus, had compassion on him and, being angered, stretched out his hand and touched him.”
items.note: The third known Old Syriac gospel manuscript, read by multispectral imaging. Cited in the ECM of Mark as a separate reading together with Ephrem.
items.source: Taylor 2020, p. 22; ECM Mark 1:41/2-10, reading h

items.name: Codex Veronensis
items.note: Read either as discomfort with an inherited iratus or as assimilation to Matthew and Luke.

items.name: Greek minuscules and one lectionary
items.note: 1358 was wrongly listed with Bezae for ὀργισθείς in Text und Textwert (1998); Jeff Cate checked the film in 2011 and found it simply omits the word. The error still circulates.
items.source: Cate 2011; Johnson 2017, p. 199; Lorenz 2021, notes; Willker

items.name: Codex Washingtonianus
items.note: Omits the end of verse 42 and all of verse 43 (καὶ ἐκαθαρίσθη … ἐξέβαλεν αὐτόν).

items.name: Codex Palatinus
items.note: Represents the oldest (African) stratum of the Latin gospels. Codex Bobiensis (k) is lacking here. Johnson lists e simply under misertus; the wording given here follows Willker and Lorenz.

items.name: Sinaitic Syriac (Old Syriac)
items.note: The Curetonian Syriac is not extant here.

takeaways: Anger is found in one Greek manuscript and one Latin text-type, centred on northern Italy from the later fourth century.
Around the same time, in Syria, Ephrem is commenting on a text that has both compassion and anger; the same double text survives in an Old Syriac manuscript.
Compassion is read everywhere else, including in the oldest branch of each version where anger appears (African Latin e; Sinaitic Syriac).

So the anger reading is not a quirk of one codex: two language areas know it by the later fourth century, with no known link between them except Tatian, who studied in Rome before working in the East.

models.intro: Four accounts of how the tradition came to look this way. Each has to explain the same facts; they differ in where the change happened and in which direction. Select a model in the top bar to see which arguments support it and which strain it.

items.title: Anger is original
items.short: Mark wrote ὀργισθείς; an early correction to σπλαγχνισθείς took over almost everywhere.

nodes.label: Early correction
nodes.note: one pious change, upstream of most later copies

nodes.label: All other Greek lines · African Latin · Sinaitic Syriac · Coptic

explains: Why anyone would change the text: anger with no stated cause is an embarrassment; compassion is the obvious repair.
Why both Matthew and Luke lack any emotion word.
The harsh tone of verse 43 (ἐμβριμησάμενος, ἐξέβαλεν).
Why anger turns up in both Latin and Syriac: both inherit an old Greek text.
costs: The correction must have happened early enough to stand upstream of every other Greek line and of the oldest Latin, Syriac and Coptic branches.
No Greek trace survives outside one bilingual codex whose Greek text is late and mixed at this very verse.
Scribes left Jesus' anger untouched at Mark 3:5 and his indignation at 10:14.

holders.name: C. H. Turner
holders.note: Harder reading; Matthew and Luke drop it as they drop μετ᾿ ὀργῆς (3:5) and ἐμβριμησάμενος.

holders.name: J. K. Elliott
holders.note: The UBS committee “allowed itself to be overwhelmed by the sheer number of MSS”.

holders.name: Morna Hooker
holders.note: “Almost certainly the correct reading.”

holders.name: Mark Proctor
holders.note: Dissertation devoted to the case for an angry Jesus.

holders.name: Joel Marcus
holders.note: σπλαγχνισθείς “is probably a scribal amelioration”.

holders.name: R. T. France
holders.note: “It is hard to see why anyone should introduce ὀργισθείς.”

holders.name: Bart Ehrman
holders.note: Once altered, the change “could easily have spread like wildfire” (p. 123). Jesus is angry that anyone would question his willingness to help (p. 138).

holders.name: H. Greeven & E. Güting
holders.note: Bezae among the witnesses preserving the ancient text here.

holders.name: M. Eugene Boring
holders.note: “A change from ‘being angry’ to ‘having compassion’ is readily explained, but not vice versa.”

holders.name: Michael Holmes (SBLGNT)
holders.note: Prints ὀργισθείς.

holders.name: NIV committee
holders.note: “Jesus was indignant.”

holders.name: Jean-Claude Haelewyck
holders.note: Variant of this model: three successive editions of the pericope, Bezae's (anger throughout) the earliest.

holders.name: Bart Bruehler
holders.note: Jesus is angry because the request threatens his preaching mission (1:38), which is what then happens (1:45).

variants.title: Lake's twist (1923)
variants.text: ὀργισθείς is original, but its subject is the leper, who touches Jesus “in a passion of rage”. Rejected by France (“an exegetical counsel of despair”), Collins and Ehrman (the subject of λέγει must be that of ἥψατο).

items.title: Compassion is original; anger is an early Greek variant
items.short: Mark wrote σπλαγχνισθείς; ὀργισθείς arose once, in the second century, in a “Western” Greek text.

nodes.label: Matthew, Luke
nodes.note: abbreviate; Matthew reuses the word at 20:34

nodes.label: All other Greek lines · African Latin · Sinaitic Syriac · Coptic
A “Western” Greek copy
nodes.note: change triggered by v. 43, or a slip on a rare word

nodes.label: Syriac harmony tradition → Ephrem, sy-F
nodes.note: anger added beside the inherited compassion

explains: The shape of the tradition: one early strand against everything else.
Why the oldest Latin (e) and the Sinaitic Syriac have compassion.
Why the Syriac form is a double reading: compassion was already there when anger arrived.
Why anger appears in both Latin and Syriac: both draw on an early Greek text, perhaps carried east by Tatian.
costs: It needs a reason for a scribe to turn compassion into anger. Proposals: the pull of ἐμβριμησάμενος in verse 43; “if you will” heard as an affront; an accidental swap of a rare word for a common look-alike.
None of these is as natural as the reverse change.
Matthew's silence at 8:3 needs explaining, since he usually keeps Mark's compassion.

holders.name: Ernst Haenchen
holders.note: Unusual among commentators in arguing strongly for σπλαγχνισθείς (so France).

holders.name: Bruce Metzger / UBS committee
holders.note: “Difficult to come to a firm decision”; swayed by the diversity and character of the evidence. Rated {B} since UBS4.

holders.name: Peter Head
holders.note: “Diverse and strong external attestation.”

holders.name: J. Donahue & D. Harrington
holders.note: Weight of the best manuscripts; anger left alone at 3:5 and 10:14; Jesus compassionate at 6:34, 8:2, 9:22.

holders.name: Adela Yarbro Collins
holders.note: Reads the scene as moving from pity (v. 41) to anger (v. 43).

holders.name: Peter J. Williams
holders.note: ὀργισθείς could arise from σπλαγχνισθείς “largely by accident”: a few letters lost in copying, then a scribe restoring the commonest word with the same ending. He grants Ephrem's support but traces it to Tatian's years in Rome (p. 3).

holders.name: NA28 / UBS5
holders.note: Print σπλαγχνισθείς.

holders.name: Tyndale House GNT
holders.note: Prints σπλαγχνισθείς.

holders.name: S. Kristianto
holders.note: Pre-genealogical coherence favours σπλαγχνισθείς.

holders.name: Editio Critica Maior, Mark
holders.note: Prints σπλαγχνισθείς with no split guiding line.

variants.title: Where Taylor 2020 fits
variants.text: D. G. K. Taylor does not decide which reading is original. His point is narrower and affects every model here: the Syriac evidence shows ὀργισθείς was a real Greek reading, not a Latin accident.

items.title: Anger arose in Latin; Bezae's Greek follows the Latin
items.short: No Greek ὀργισθείς ever existed before Bezae: iratus arose inside the Latin tradition and Bezae's Greek column was conformed to it.

nodes.label: The whole Greek tradition · Syriac · Coptic
Italian Old Latin (a, ff², r¹, d)
Bezae's Greek column
nodes.note: Greek conformed to a Latin model

nodes.label: Ephrem, sy-F
nodes.note: unexplained by this model: needs coincidence or Latin–Syriac contact

explains: Why no other Greek manuscript has ὀργισθείς.
Why the Latin witnesses to iratus belong to a single text-type and region.
Why the Latin tradition is so unsettled at this word: eight different forms and four verbs across eleven witnesses.
It matches a wider pattern: Lorenz counts 410 readings in Bezae's Mark that agree with the Latin against the Greek mainstream.
costs: The Syriac evidence. Ephrem and the Old Syriac palimpsest know “being angered” in a region with no Latin gospels.
The autem misertus → autem iratus slip does not fit: the anger manuscripts read Et iratus. Johnson's main proposal, miseratus → iratus, avoids this objection but still leaves the Syriac unexplained.
The direction of influence between Bezae's columns is disputed; Lorenz himself left it open in 2016.

holders.name: J. Rendel Harris
holders.note: An ambiguous Latin motus, later resolved as misertus or iratus, with Bezae's Greek retranslated.

holders.name: Peter J. Williams (blog)
holders.note: Suggested autem miser(a)tus → autem iratus; later preferred a Greek-internal accident.

holders.name: Jeff Cate
holders.note: Latin has no verb equivalent to σπλαγχνίζομαι; the variant “arose in Latin”.

holders.name: Peter Lorenz
holders.note: The anger witnesses reduce to one insular Latin tradition; “we are essentially counting the same Greek witness over and over.”

holders.name: James Snapp
holders.note: Bezae's Greek retranslated from Latin.

holders.name: Nathan Johnson
holders.note: iratus arose from miseratus by loss of letters (MISERATUS → ISERATUS → IRATUS); Bezae's scribe, who struggled with σπλαγχνίζομαι, conformed his Greek to the Latin; Ephrem's “anger” is explained from verse 43 (pp. 189–91, 195, 199–201).

holders.name: Peter Lorenz (monograph)
holders.note: Bezae's Greek text of Mark was corrected towards a Latin model at the end of the fourth century.

variants.title: Written before the Syriac palimpsest was known
variants.text: Lorenz and Johnson argued that all support for anger is tied to Latin. Williams granted Ephrem's support but suggested that Tatian, who had studied in Rome, might have drawn on early Latin renderings. Taylor published the Old Syriac text in 2020.

items.title: An Aramaic source: “angry” was the first Greek wording, “compassion” restores the sense
items.short: Yastrebov, building on Casey. The Aramaic behind the story had regaz, a word that can mean “was angry” or “was deeply stirred”. Mark first rendered it ὀργισθείς; Mark himself or an early editor then corrected it to σπλαγχνισθείς, and the corrected form became the ancestor of almost all copies.

nodes.label: Aramaic source: רגז regaz
nodes.note: “seethed”, “was deeply stirred” — in which sense, unknown

nodes.label: Ancestor of nearly all Greek manuscripts and versions
The first form survives in a “Western” strand
nodes.note: implied by the lecture, not drawn in its diagram

explains: Why “angry” stands in the story at all without any stated cause: it is a translator's choice between two senses of one word, not a report of Jesus' mood.

Why σπλαγχνισθείς fits the scene so well. On this account it is not a lucky substitute but a deliberate correction back to what the source meant — which answers Williams's “too convenient” objection to the anger reading.
Why the change needs no embarrassed scribes. The motive is accuracy, so it does not matter that copyists elsewhere leave Jesus' anger alone.
Why Matthew and Luke have no emotion word, if they knew the first form.

Why nearly every witness has compassion: a revised edition, not a scattering of scribal changes, stands at the head of the tradition. The lecture's wider point is that an early revision which became the ancestor of everything “will look to us like the initial text”.
costs: The second sense of regaz. Trembling, agitation and distress are attested for the root; “stirred with pity” specifically is not securely so. The ordinary Aramaic and Syriac word for compassion is from rḥm, which is what the Syriac Gospels use here.
It needs a written Aramaic source behind this story, which many doubt for Mark.

It needs two forms of Mark, with the earlier one surviving only in one “Western” strand. Yet Bezae, the single Greek witness, has a late and mixed text at this verse and probably took the word from its Latin page.
Like Model A, it requires the correction to stand upstream of every other Greek line and of the oldest Latin, Syriac and Coptic.
It cannot be tested against any surviving document — a limit the lecture itself states plainly: this may recover “the history of the wording, but not yet the history of the meaning”.

holders.name: Maurice Casey
holders.note: “The Aramaic source will have read regaz. This word often does mean ‘be angry’, which is why Mark translated it with orgistheis. But the Aramaic regaz has a wider range of meaning … including ‘tremble’ and ‘be deeply moved’.” Mark “did not mean that Jesus was angry”: he suffered from bilingual interference (Jesus of Nazareth, p. 63).

holders.name: Gleb Yastrebov
holders.note: Simplifies Casey: no unusual meaning of ὀργίζομαι in Mark's mind is needed, only an ordinary wrong choice between two senses, later corrected by Mark or his first editors. Offered as one competing scenario, not a proof.

variants.title: How this differs from Casey
variants.text: Casey holds that Mark wrote ὀργισθείς and meant “deeply moved” by it; the Greek word is original and no correction is involved. Yastrebov finds that needlessly complicated: Mark simply chose the wrong sense, and the tradition's σπλαγχνισθείς is the repair.

variants.title: How this differs from the older Aramaic theory
variants.text: The theory dismissed under T4 confuses two different words that look alike (ethraḥam / ethraʿem). This one involves a single word with two senses and a translator's choice, so the objections to T4 do not touch it.

variants.title: Details in the lecture to correct
variants.text: (1) it r¹ is Codex Usserianus Primus (Dublin, c. 600), not Codex Schlettstadtensis. (2) The Diatessaron does not prove that “angry” alone stood in a mid-second-century text: Ephrem's text had both words, and the Arabic Diatessaron has compassion. (3) Bezae's Latin column probably does not “confirm” its Greek; the Greek more likely follows the Latin (Johnson 2017; Lorenz 2021). (4) The footnote reproduced from Keener as a list of scholars who prefer “angry” begins “Favoring this reading” and names Metzger, Stein, Donahue and Harrington, Collins, Lorenz and Johnson — all defenders of compassion. (5) Casey's Jesus of Nazareth appeared in 2010, not 2008. (6) To add: the Old Syriac palimpsest published by Taylor 2020, which postdates UBS5.

arguments.intro: Each argument is given with the case for it, the replies, and where the reasoning currently stands. The markers show how each one bears on the four transmission models.

groups.title: External evidence
groups.question: What do the manuscripts and versions themselves tell us?

items.title: Compassion has the breadth
items.claim: σπλαγχνισθείς is read in every Greek text-form and in every ancient version.

pro.text: The UBS committee was moved by “the diversity and character of evidence”, not by numbers.
The oldest branch of each version where anger appears still has compassion: the African Latin (e) and the Sinaitic Syriac.
The Greek tradition shows no disturbance at this point — no marginal notes, corrections or mixed forms.

contra.text: Manuscripts must be weighed, not counted; slender support says nothing about a reading's merits.

Once a scribe made the change, it “could easily have spread like wildfire … until the original text came to be virtually lost except in a few surviving sources.” No manuscript of the verse is older than Vaticanus, nearly three centuries after Mark.

items.status: Strong, but not decisive on its own: it shows where the readings were, not which came first.

items.title: How many witnesses for anger are there really?
items.claim: The four Latin manuscripts and Bezae's Greek are not five witnesses but one tradition.

pro.text: Latin manuscripts that share a rendering go back to one translation and count once. The evidence “is equivalent to no more than two Greek witnesses”.
a, d, ff² and r¹ share one text-type, the “Western” gospel order and a northern Italian milieu of c. 350–380.

contra.text: Even on this count the reading reaches back before c. 350, earlier than any Greek manuscript of the verse except ℵ and B.
The Old Syriac palimpsest and Ephrem add a second, non-Latin region.

items.status: The Latin witnesses do collapse into one. The Syriac evidence, published later, is what keeps the anger reading from being purely local. Even the Syriac counts as separate only if it did not reach Syria from the same Western text, for example through Tatian (see “The Syriac evidence”).

items.title: Is Bezae an independent Greek witness?
items.claim: Bezae's Greek text of Mark is late and mixed, and at this verse it may simply follow the Latin.

pro.text: Lorenz assigns 410 readings in Bezae's Mark to a “Latin layer”, 332 of them with no other Greek support; ὀργισθείς is in that list.
In the same clause Bezae reads αὐτοῦ ἥψατο αὐτοῦ, which combines the reading of ℵ B with the majority reading — a sign of a text that developed after both.
Bezae sides with ℵ B for καί at the start of the verse, then departs from all Greek manuscripts in the next word.

The scribe misspells σπλαγχνίζομαι in 7 of those 11 places but has no such trouble with ὀργίζομαι or with comparable verbs. A parallel case of Latin influence: at 3:5 Bezae alone reads νεκρώσει, evidently from the Latin emortua.

contra.text: Bezae preserves weakly attested original readings elsewhere in Mark, and 1:41 is one of them.
Readings of D supported by the Old Latin “are evidently part of a much older tradition” and should not be treated as singular.
Wholesale Latinization of Bezae's Greek is not accepted, though in places it remains the best explanation.

Bezae's scribe keeps σπλαγχνίζομαι in all eleven other Gospel occurrences, so he was not avoiding the word. (Johnson's claim is narrower: the scribe changed it only here, where his Latin read iratus.)

items.status: Bezae on its own proves little either way. Johnson's spelling data make the Latin the likeliest source of Bezae's own ὀργισθείς, which fits every model here. The case for an early Greek ὀργισθείς rests on the Latin–Syriac agreement, not on Bezae.

items.title: The Syriac evidence
items.claim: Ephrem and an Old Syriac manuscript attest “being angered” outside the Latin world.

pro.text: The palimpsest reads “had compassion on him and, being angered, stretched out his hand” — “precisely the double reading that Ephrem was attempting to explain”.
Ephrem cites the gospel word itself (“Our Lord was angry, therefore”); mistranslation in the standard editions hid this.
Agreements between Syriac and Old Latin against the Greek majority are best explained by “a lost common Greek reading”.

The same rare root, as mpār, stands in the Old Syriac palimpsest at Mark 1:41 itself, and the verb “is regularly used in Syriac with the meaning ‘to be angry, angered’”. Johnson's two objections were written before this was known.

Ephrem reports other interpreters who explained the anger differently, some saying it was directed at the leprosy itself (Commentary 12.23). The anger was in a text they shared, not a device of Ephrem's own.
Ephrem's students edited and added to the Commentary in two stages, so arguments from the consistency of its wording are insecure.

contra.text: Ephrem's anger word (root pwr) is rare and is not the usual Syriac equivalent of ὀργίζομαι, which is rgez; and Ephrem “never in fact quotes ‘anger’ from his text”.
Ephrem's talk of anger is anti-Marcionite rhetoric, not a citation. (Taylor: “a clever argument … quite implausible”.)
Ephrem ties the anger to the rebuke and dismissal of verses 43–44, using the Syriac word that renders ἐμβριμησάμενος there; his language “is fully accounted for by ἐμβριμησάμενος”.
contra.ref: Lake 1923, p. 197 n. 1, quoted in Johnson 2017, p. 190

contra.text: The Syriac form is a double reading. It presupposes a text with compassion and so is not evidence for anger instead of compassion.

If Tatian, who studied in Rome, brought the reading east in his harmony, the Syriac is not a second independent region but the same Western strand, carried to Syria by one man. The reading would still have to be in the Gospel text Tatian used by c. 170, almost certainly a Greek one, since Roman Christians then wrote in Greek and the Latin Gospels are later. Its spread east and west would no longer count as separate witnesses. (This route is inferred from Tatian's career; no ancient source says so.)

items.status: This is the newest evidence and the least absorbed in the literature. One point is still open: how the palimpsest renders verse 43 has not been published, so it is not yet certain that “being angered” translates ὀργισθείς and not a displaced ἐμβριμησάμενος. Against displacement: Ephrem uses both the rebuke word of verse 43 and the separate anger word, which suggests his text had both.

items.title: The witnesses that have neither word
items.claim: Some copies drop the participle altogether.

pro.text: The absence of either word in Old Latin b suggests a copyist found iratus and removed it.

contra.text: The Greek omitters are late Byzantine copies whose exemplars certainly read σπλαγχνισθείς; they are assimilating to Matthew and Luke.
If scribes were troubled by anger they would omit, as these do — not substitute a different emotion.
Minuscule 1358, often cited for ὀργισθείς, in fact omits.
The omissions in b and in lectionary 866 need not be deliberate: “the tendency of manuscripts to omit words accidentally is a sufficient explanation.”

items.status: Ambiguous. Only b is close enough to the anger witnesses for its silence to mean anything.

items.title: The Latin tradition is unsettled here
items.claim: Eleven Latin witnesses show eight different forms and four different verbs.

pro.text: Latin had no single verb for σπλαγχνίζομαι, so translators improvised — fertile ground for a stray rendering.

contra.text: The same variety could be successive corrections away from an inherited iratus: c and q may have been corrected to the Vulgate.

items.status: Shows that something happened in Latin, not what.

groups.title: What would scribes do?
groups.question: Which change is easier to imagine a copyist making?

items.title: The harder reading
items.claim: Scribes would turn anger into compassion, never the reverse.

pro.text: “Scribes might well have changed a statement that Jesus felt anger to one that he felt compassion, but it is difficult to see why they should have made the opposite change.”
The reading “is so striking and ‘improbable’ that a correction to the ‘safer’ σπλαγχνισθείς would be very natural”.

Origen, using Stoic theory, allows Jesus and his followers only the first stirrings of emotion (propatheia), not full grief or anger. An angry Jesus needed explaining to philosophically minded readers.

contra.text: Copyists left Jesus' anger at Mark 3:5 and his indignation at 10:14 alone.
Scribes sometimes added anger: ἐν ὀργῇ at Luke 6:10 (Bezae and others) and ἐπιτιμήσας at Mark 10:14 (W Θ and others). Nowhere in the manuscripts of Mark is Jesus' anger censored.

σπλαγχνίζομαι never occurs as a deponent in the Septuagint, while ὀργίζομαι is common there. By Ehrman's own rule that “readers typically confuse unusual words for common ones”, a slip from compassion to anger is the likelier one.
Interpreters ancient and modern explain the anger so readily that its difficulty is “overstated”.
If anger fits the rebuke of verse 43, then on narrative grounds it is no longer the harder reading — compassion is.

rejoinder.text: At 3:5 and 10:14 “there was obvious cause for anger”; here there is none, which is why only this one was changed.

items.status: The strongest single argument for anger, and the reason most commentators adopt it. Its premise — that early scribes were embarrassed by an angry Jesus — is contested, since elsewhere they add anger and never remove it.

items.title: An accidental swap in Greek
items.claim: ὀργισθείς replaced σπλαγχνισθείς by a copying slip.

pro.text: In early capitals the two words end with the same six letters, begin with the same curved stroke (Ο, Ϲ) and share a Γ. ὀργισθείς is the commonest biblical form in -ισθείς, while the verb σπλαγχνίζομαι is absent from the Septuagint.
A two-step route: a few letters lost by eye-skip (ΠΛΑ or ΧΝ), then a later scribe making sense of Ϲ…ΓΙϹΘΕΙϹ as the familiar ΟΡΓΙϹΘΕΙϹ.
If anger were original, it would be a remarkable coincidence that a substitute existed which is both a perfect contextual fit and graphically similar.
The word did trouble copyists. Bezae's scribe misspells it in 7 of its 11 other Gospel occurrences, e.g. σπλαχνίζομαι (Mark 8:2), ἐσπλαγχίσθη (Luke 10:33) and a corrected false start at Mark 6:34.

contra.text: ΟΡΓ- is far shorter than ΣΠΛΑΓΧΝ-; the words do not look alike.
Proposals of accidental change are “unconvincing”.

items.status: The best-developed route from compassion to anger. It supplies a mechanism without a motive, and it answers the objection that the two words differ in length.

items.title: Pulled in from verse 43
items.claim: Anger in verse 41 was suggested by ἐμβριμησάμενος two verses later.

pro.text: One of the origins the UBS committee considered.
Ephrem shows how an ancient reader got there: “in response to ‘if you will’ he was angered”.

contra.text: A copyist would more likely change what he was writing in light of what he had already copied, not what came two verses later; and why not change verse 43 itself?
The same link is used the other way: verse 43 shows the anger of verse 41 is at home in the story.
Even Williams, who defends compassion, judges this explanation “slim”.
With a dative and following speech, ἐμβριμάομαι means a stern order, not an emotion, which gives verse 43 less pull toward anger.

items.status: Doubted on both sides. It survives mainly as the way ancient readers such as Ephrem made sense of the scene.

items.title: A confusion in Aramaic or Syriac
items.claim: ethraḥam (“he had pity”) and ethraʿem (“he was enraged”) differ by one guttural.

pro.text: Proposed by Zahn (Aramaic) and Rendel Harris (Syriac); listed by Metzger; still mentioned by Marcus.

contra.text: No Aramaic Mark is known to have existed.
The anger word the Syriac tradition actually has is mpār, not ethraʿem.
Ehrman and Williams, on opposite sides, both judge it improbable.

items.status: Now effectively ruled out by the Syriac evidence itself.

items.title: A slip in Latin
items.claim: iratus arose inside the Latin tradition.

pro.text: An ambiguous motus resolved two ways (Harris 1891); or autem miser(a)tus → autem iratus by loss of letters (Williams 2007).
Or simple loss of letters followed by repair: MISERATUS → ISERATUS → IRATUS. The correction in r¹ shows the same step run backwards.

contra.text: The anger manuscripts read Et iratus, not autem iratus; misertus goes with Iesus autem.
It cannot account for the Syriac.

items.status: The autem route does not fit the wording (Et iratus). Loss of letters from miseratus remains possible within Latin, but cannot account for the Syriac.

items.title: One Aramaic word with two senses
items.claim: The source had regaz; “angry” is a translator's choice of the wrong sense, and “compassion” corrects it.

pro.text: “The Aramaic regaz has a wider range of meaning than ‘be angry’, including ‘tremble’ and ‘be deeply moved’.” Mark's Greek here is “a literal and unrevised translation of an Aramaic source”.
pro.ref: Casey 2010, p. 63, as reproduced in Yastrebov 2026

pro.text: A simpler form: the source meant “was stirred”; Mark took the commoner sense and wrote ὀργισθείς; Mark or his first editors then corrected it. This needs only an ordinary mistranslation.
Ancient texts were routinely revised by their authors and heirs, and an early revised form that became the ancestor of the whole tradition would be indistinguishable, for us, from the original.
It explains the perfect fit of σπλαγχνισθείς, which defenders of compassion press against the anger reading, without appeal to coincidence.

contra.text: The senses attested for the root are trembling, agitation and anger. “Moved with pity” is a further step; the regular word for that is from rḥm, as in every Syriac version of this verse.
The Syriac tradition, which uses rgez as its normal word for ὀργίζομαι, does not use it here; its anger word is mpār.
Explanations from Aramaic are judged improbable by scholars on both sides, though they have the older two-word theory in view.
A first edition surviving only through Bezae is hard to square with the late, mixed and Latin-dependent character of Bezae's Greek at this verse.

rejoinder.text: The lecture claims no more than a possible history of the wording: “we are dealing not with proofs but with competing scenarios.”

items.status: The most economical account of how both words could be early, and the only anger-first theory that explains why compassion fits. It stands or falls on whether regaz can bear the sense required.

groups.title: Matthew and Luke
groups.question: The two earliest readers of Mark both have no emotion here. What does that show?

table.caption: What Matthew and Luke do with Mark's emotion words for Jesus

items.title: Both evangelists drop the word
items.claim: Matthew and Luke read ὀργισθείς in Mark and removed it, as they always remove Jesus' anger.

pro.text: “Matthew and Luke have no qualms about describing Jesus as compassionate. But they never describe him as angry. In fact, whenever one of their sources, Mark, did so, they both independently rewrite the term out of their stories.”
If σπλαγχνισθείς were original they “would probably have included it”, since both use the term of Jesus elsewhere (Matt 9:36; Luke 7:13).

contra.text: Luke drops every Markan σπλαγχνίζομαι, so his silence here proves nothing. Ehrman himself notes that Luke recasts 6:34 and lacks 8:2.
Both also drop συλλυπούμενος (grief) at 3:5 and the plea for compassion at 9:22: “why would Matthew and Luke censor sympathy and mercy?”
Both also drop Jesus' love for the rich man (Mark 10:21): they remove warm emotions as well as harsh ones.
Both omit all of verse 43 too, and this pericope has a cluster of other Matthew–Luke agreements against Mark (ἥψατο αὐτοῦ λέγων, εὐθέως). The shared omission is part of a larger pattern.
The argument assumes Matthew and Luke edited Mark independently; if Luke knew Matthew, this is one agreement, not two.
The argument refuses one coincidence (that both happened to omit the word) while accepting another (that both, independently, chose omission as their remedy).

items.status: Weaker than usually stated. Only Matthew's silence carries weight, and Matthew is abbreviating heavily here.

items.title: Matthew reuses the scene elsewhere
items.claim: Matthew's two healings of blind men borrow the vocabulary of Mark 1:41–45, including σπλαγχνισθείς.

pro.text: Matt 20:34 adds σπλαγχνισθεὶς … ἥψατο … εὐθέως to a Markan healing that has none of it — a sequence “found in no other antecedent Greek literature”, pointing to Matthew's knowledge of σπλαγχνισθείς in Mark 1:41.
Its doublet, Matt 9:30–31, has ἐνεβριμήθη, “see that no one knows” and διεφήμισαν — the vocabulary of Mark 1:43–45. Ehrman too judges Matt 9:30 “dependent on this passage in Mark”.
pro.ref: from the Greek texts; Ehrman 2003, p. 133

contra.text: σπλαγχνίζομαι is a favourite of Matthew's in any case (9:36; 18:27), so 20:34 need not depend on Mark 1:41.
Matthew “consistently keeps Markan ‘compassion’ language”, which makes its absence at 8:3 all the more striking.

items.status: Suggestive evidence that Matthew's copy of Mark had σπλαγχνισθείς.

groups.title: Mark's own story
groups.question: Which reading fits the passage and the Gospel?

items.title: The harshness of verse 43
items.claim: ἐμβριμησάμενος and ἐξέβαλεν show the scene is angry throughout.

pro.text: ἐμβριμάομαι is the snorting of a horse; of people, “to express indignation by an explosive expulsion of breath”. There is no reason to deny the nuance of anger here.
ἐξέβαλεν is the word used for casting out demons (1:34, 39).
The harsh words of v. 43 “cohere with the minority reading of v. 41”.

ἐμβριμάομαι means to rebuke or reproach, as at 14:5; and ἐκβάλλω in Mark is used “of some kind of aggressive action” in every instance. It is easier to understand a severe rebuke if Jesus was angry than if he felt sorry for the man.

contra.text: The story can as well be read as a shift: pity in v. 41, stern dismissal in v. 43.
ἐκβάλλω is not always violent in Mark (1:12; 5:40).
The same harshness is what would lead a copyist to write anger in v. 41 (see “Pulled in from verse 43”).

With a dative and following speech, ἐμβριμάομαι denotes a forceful order or rebuke (LXX Dan 11:30; Matt 9:30; Mark 14:5), not an inner state; the “snorting” sense belongs to uses without speech. A defender of anger concedes that verse 43 does not itself show it.

items.status: Cuts both ways: coherence for one side, a source of contamination for the other.

items.title: Angry at what?
items.claim: If Jesus is angry, the text does not say why.

options.text: At the leper's “if you will”, as doubting his willingness
At the disease and the evil power behind it
At the purity system that excluded the man
At being asked to usurp the priest's role of declaring him clean
At the interruption of his preaching mission
options.who: Bruehler (after Lane, Loader); rejected by Hooker, France, Ehrman

options.text: It is the leper who is angry

pro.text: The lack of an obvious object is precisely what would provoke a correction.

contra.text: A reading that needs six competing explanations may simply be a mistake.
Or the reverse: if explanations come so easily, the reading was never very difficult.
In no other Markan story is Jesus angry with the person asking for help; he is patient even with the doubting father of 9:22–24, while this leper is sure he can heal.

Mark's narrative supplies the cause: Jesus has just left the Capernaum crowds to preach elsewhere (1:38) when a public request for a spectacular cure threatens to bring them back, as it does (1:45; 2:1–2). The anger is at the situation, not the man.

ἐάν θέλῃς is a prospective condition that expects fulfilment; it is not used to question the subject's willingness, and Matthew and Luke keep it. This tells against the view that the leper doubted Jesus.

items.status: No agreed answer among those who accept anger. The fullest recent case (Bruehler) finds the cause in Mark's own narrative, but the easier the anger is to explain, the weaker the harder-reading argument becomes.

items.title: Mark's usage
items.claim: Both emotions are at home in Mark's portrait of Jesus.

pro.text: Compassion: 6:34; 8:2; 9:22 — NA28's own marginal references at 1:41.
Anger and indignation: 3:5; 10:14. Mark's Jesus also sighs (7:34; 8:12) and is distressed (14:33).

items.status: Mark's style does not decide the question.

positions.intro: Critical editions mostly print compassion; commentators mostly argue for anger; the specialist text-critical articles of 2012–2018 mostly defend compassion.

items.name: NET (current)
items.note: “Moved with indignation”; the first edition read compassion

items.name: Beavis (Paideia)
items.note: presents both; notes v. 43 coheres with anger

items.name: Yastrebov
items.note: as Mark's first wording, later corrected to compassion

items.claim: “Minuscule 1358 reads ὀργισθείς.”
items.fact: It omits the word. The citation is an error in Text und Textwert (1998), corrected by Cate in 2011.

items.claim: “Anger is supported only in Latin-speaking areas.”
items.fact: Ephrem and the Old Syriac palimpsest (published 2020) attest it in Syria. The one known bridge between the two worlds is Tatian.

items.claim: “Ephrem read anger instead of compassion.”
items.fact: His text, like the palimpsest, had both.

items.claim: “Ephrem never actually quotes ‘anger’ from his gospel text.”
items.fact: He cites mpār, the very word that stands in the Old Syriac palimpsest at this verse (Taylor 2020).

items.claim: “Four or five independent witnesses support anger.”
items.fact: The Latin manuscripts are one text-type; Bezae's Greek may depend on it.

items.claim: “The UBS committee simply followed the majority.”
items.fact: Metzger cites the diversity and character of the evidence, not its quantity.

items.claim: “The UBS rating is {D}.”
items.fact: That was UBS3. It has been {B} since UBS4.

items.claim: “Many manuscripts read compassion” (NIV footnote).
“iratus came from autem misertus by a copying slip.”
items.fact: The manuscripts with iratus read Et iratus. (Johnson's different proposal, miseratus → iratus by loss of letters, is not affected.)

items.claim: “Lake argued for an angry Jesus.”
items.fact: He made the leper the subject of ὀργισθείς.

assessment.title: The most likely story
assessment.label: A provisional judgment, offered for discussion
assessment.verdict: Mark most probably wrote “moved with compassion”. “Angry” is a very early alternative, about a century younger than the Gospel, that travelled both west and east.
assessment.odds: Roughly two to one for compassion — a judgment, not a calculation.

steps.text: One Greek copy, probably in or near Rome, comes to read ὀργισθείς, “angry” — most likely under the pull of the stern verse 43, perhaps helped by a slip on a rare word.
Tatian, who studied in Rome, carries the reading east in his Gospel harmony. In Italy it enters the Latin translation as iratus.
In Syria, “angry” meets the ordinary Syriac Gospels, which say “had compassion”, and the two are combined: the text Ephrem explains and the palimpsest preserves.
Codex Bezae takes “angry” from its Latin page into its Greek. A corrector removes iratus from the last Latin manuscript around 600.
The Greek copy that began it leaves no descendants. Every other Greek manuscript, and the oldest Latin and Syriac translations, keep what Mark wrote.

weakLinks: No fully convincing reason has been found for a copyist to turn compassion into anger. The reverse change is easier to imagine, and that remains the best argument for anger. Model D answers exactly this point, at the price of an Aramaic source and a first edition of Mark.
That Tatian carried the reading east is inferred from his biography. No ancient source says so.
wouldChange: How the Old Syriac palimpsest words verse 43. If it has the ordinary “rebuked” there, its “being angered” in verse 41 is a true rendering of ὀργισθείς and anger gains ground. If not, the Syriac evidence falls away.
A second Greek manuscript with ὀργισθείς, or a papyrus of Mark 1 — none survives for this verse.
closing: Whichever word Mark wrote, both were read as Scripture: Ephrem expounded a Jesus who was angered, while the Greek-speaking churches heard of one moved with compassion. And the story itself holds both notes — a Jesus who touches the untouchable in verse 41 and sends him off sternly in verse 43. The variant sharpens a tension that Mark's text has either way.

The case is also a good picture of how the New Testament text is studied. Counting manuscripts settles nothing; one codex against sixteen hundred is not the real contest. The work is to ask where each reading was known, how it could have travelled, and which change a copyist was likelier to make — and then to say plainly how sure one is. Here the honest answer is: fairly, not fully. A page of erased Syriac at Sinai may yet decide it.
